description.content:
Every Qeet ID API call, one folder per API document and bounded context. Generated by make postman from
api/openapi/*.yaml: edit the API sources in api/openapi/src, not this file.

To call a local server (make dev), import qeet-id-local.postman_environment.json too and select it.
Sign up or sign in first: the answer fills bearerToken, and creating a resource fills its id variable,
such as organizationID. api/postman/README.md has the details.

Qeet ID — Authentication & Access API

Human authentication, passkeys, MFA, and authorization for Qeet ID.

## Start here

1. Authenticate a user — password login, or passwordless **passkey** login. Passkeys are first-class: a user can exist with no password at all.
2. Satisfy **MFA** if organization policy or adaptive risk requires it. A registered passkey satisfies MFA on its own.
3. Use the returned `Bearer` access token for authenticated calls.
4. **Signup creates an organization-less user.** Create an organization via the Identity Management API before any organization-scoped call — the creator becomes the organization owner.
5. Configure authorization: RBAC is the baseline; layer in ABAC, ReBAC, or AuthZEN as needed.

## Authentication

Auth modes: `bearerAuth` (user/service JWT), `apiKeyAuth` (`Authorization: ApiKey <key>` — legacy scheme), `scimBearer` (per-organization SCIM token), `clientCredentials` (OAuth M2M), and `ssoCookie` (hosted-login SSO session). CSRF protection applies only to cookie sessions (`ssoCookie`): requests authorised by `bearerAuth` or `apiKeyAuth` bypass it, as do the token endpoint (POST /v1/oauth/token) and the directory sign-in (POST /ldap/{id}/authenticate), which carry their credentials in the request. Basic credentials do not bypass it. A request that fails the check is refused with 403 `csrf_failed`.

The responses of the sign-up, sign-in (password, MFA, magic link, passkey), refresh, organization-switch, sign-out (hosted session, everywhere) and forgot-password operations, and of those returning a new authenticator secret, recovery codes, pairing code or device credential, are sent with `Cache-Control: no-store` and `Pragma: no-cache`.

Every response carries an `X-Request-Id` header naming the request; quote it when reporting a problem. An error body repeats it as `error.request_id`. A path with an encoded slash or backslash (`%2F`, `%5C`) is refused with 400 `bad_request`.

## Related APIs

- **Identity Management API** — organizations, users, groups, invitations
- **Federation API** — OIDC/OAuth provider, SAML, SCIM, LDAP, social
- **Developer API** — API keys, agents, webhooks, vaults
- **Operations API** — audit, analytics, billing

## Contract maintenance

This document covers routes mounted by internal/bootstrap/router.go. internal/bootstrap/openapi_coverage_test.go walks the production mount helpers and fails when a mounted operation is undocumented, a documented operation is stale, or API-auth security declarations disagree with runtime classification.

item.description: Login, signup, refresh, sessions, hosted-login SSO cookie.

description.content: Sends a password-reset link to the supplied email when it belongs to an account. It always returns a neutral confirmation regardless of whether the address exists, so it cannot be used to enumerate accounts, and it is rate limited. The link is stored and emailed after the answer, so the answer is the same for any address, takes the same minimum time, and does not depend on whether the email could be delivered. Complete the flow with the reset-password call using the token from the emailed link. The link goes to the address as the account stores it, not as typed, and ends the account's earlier reset links. An address may ask three times, then once every five minutes (429 too_many_requests past that, whether or not it has an account). A completed reset, a password change or set, an email change and anything else that ends the person's sign-ins also ends their unused reset and magic links. A request for an account is recorded in its organization's audit trail as auth.password_reset_requested (at most ten per account, then one a minute). On a domain whose organization requires single sign-on, the request is refused with 403 auth.sso_required once counted against the per-address bound, before any account is looked up, and no link is sent (see the SSORequired response).

response.name: Accepted (always, to avoid account enumeration); returns a neutral confirmation message

description.content: no-store: the response carries a token, a secret or a sign-in session, so no cache may keep it. (This can only be one of no-store)
no-cache, the same instruction for HTTP/1.0 caches. (This can only be one of no-cache)

Authenticates a user by email and password and, on success, returns an access and refresh token pair. If the account has a second factor enrolled, tokens are withheld and a short-lived mfa_token with the available methods is returned instead; exchange it for tokens at the complete-MFA call. Passwordless accounts authenticate through passkey login rather than this endpoint, and a registered passkey satisfies MFA on its own. Requests are rate limited to slow credential stuffing. Failed sign-ins are counted per account and source network, per account across networks, and per source network across accounts (see the sign-in lockout on the create-SSO-session call); a locked account answers 429 auth.account_locked whatever the password, a throttled source 429 too_many_requests, and an address with no account answers exactly like a wrong password. A suspended or otherwise inactive account also answers a wrong password with 401 auth.invalid_credentials, counted like any wrong password; only the right password is refused with 403 auth.account_inactive. When the account's own organization has switched password sign-in off, a correct password is refused with 403 auth.method_disabled. Every sign-in is assessed for risk (bot-like clients, and impossible travel and new devices where the organization turns them on), and its country and device are kept 90 days for later sign-ins to be compared against. A risky sign-in by someone with no second factor answers an mfa_token challenge met by a code sent to their verified email address (methods [email], the factor named by the challenge's own id), or 403 auth.risk_verification_unavailable when they have no verified address. While the organization's address rules are on, a sign-in from an address they refuse is refused with 403 auth.address_not_allowed before any session is issued; the same holds on every other way of signing in to the organization (passkey, magic link, social, SAML, LDAP, invitation, organization switch, application authorization and the device flow). Each failed attempt is recorded in the audit trail of the organization the sign-in was for (or the account's own) as auth.sign_in_failed: the account, or no one for an address with no account, the reason (wrong_password, unknown_account, account_locked or source_throttled) and the source, never what was submitted. The records are bounded per source network and per organization (sign_in_failures_unrecorded_total counts the rest). A lock a failure sets is recorded as auth.account_locked with locked_until, when it lifts; a source throttle as auth.source_throttled. On a domain whose organization requires single sign-on, the sign-in is refused with 403 auth.sso_required before any account is looked up or password checked, and nothing is counted against the lockout (see the SSORequired response).

response.name:
Either a full token pair (no MFA) or an MFA challenge to complete at
POST /v1/auth/mfa — when the user holds a second factor, or must have
one (see MFAChallenge).

Exchanges the mfa_token from /v1/auth/login, plus exactly one proof from the factors the challenge listed, for a token pair: a code, a passkey assertion, or an approved push. An enrolment challenge is completed instead by a code from the authenticator app set up for it (POST /v1/auth/mfa/enroll) — the response then carries the account's new recovery codes, shown once — or skipped while its grace period runs. A wrong proof counts against the challenge's and the account's attempt budgets. A wrong proof is recorded in the organization's audit trail as auth.sign_in_failed (method mfa, reason code_invalid, with the proof kind and the attempts left). Fifty wrong proofs in a row, however far apart, lock the person's second-factor sign-in: that answer and every later one is 403 mfa.locked, even with the right proof, the lock is audited as auth.mfa_locked and the person is emailed. A right proof ends a shorter run; a password reset, a password change or set, or an administrator's reset of their factors lifts the lock.

response.name: Second factor verified (or, for an enrolment challenge, set up or put off); token pair issued, with recovery_codes when an authenticator app was just set up.

description.content: no-store: the response carries a token, a secret or a sign-in session, so no cache may keep it. (This can only be one of no-store)
no-cache, the same instruction for HTTP/1.0 caches. (This can only be one of no-cache)

Sends a code to one of the challenged person's email or SMS factors (factor_id, from the challenge's factors), to complete the challenge with. At most five per challenge (429). Used by both sign-in flows. For a risky sign-in by someone with no second factor, the challenge's one factor is their verified email address, named by the challenge's own id: send its code here with factor_id set to the mfa_token, then submit it to complete the challenge. A code to one factor can be sent at most every 30 seconds, ten an hour to one person and five an hour to one address or number over every account; past that the call answers 429 mfa.code_send_limited with retry_after (seconds). A new code makes the factor's earlier unused code stop working. A code sent here only completes a sign-in, never a step-up. An SMS code needs an organization whose plan includes SMS (403 upgrade_required). Each code sent is audited as mfa.otp_sent.
Starts a passkey assertion for the challenged person's own passkeys; only an assertion from this ceremony completes the challenge. Used by both sign-in flows.

Sends a sign-in approval request to the challenged person's push devices; only its approval completes the challenge, and only once. Complete with push: true. Used by both sign-in flows. Each phone is sent a high-priority push that lives as long as the request can be answered (two minutes); a phone the push service reports as no longer having the app is retired. When the request reaches none of the person's phones it is closed and the call answers 502 mfa.push_delivery_failed, so the person can use another way to verify. The answer carries a two-digit number to show on the sign-in screen: the phone must send it back to approve. A person is sent at most five requests in ten minutes, and none for the rest of an hour in which they denied three; past that the call answers 429 mfa.push_limited.

item.name: Set up an authenticator app to sign in

request.name: Set up an authenticator app to sign in

description.content: For an enrolment challenge — the account must have a second factor and holds none — starts an authenticator app and returns its secret and otpauth:// provisioning URL. A code from the app then completes the challenge (POST /v1/auth/mfa or /v1/auth/session/mfa). Calling again replaces the app not yet confirmed. Refused (400) for a challenge that is not an enrolment one; answers mfa challenge expired once the account holds a factor. Used by both sign-in flows.
no-store: the response carries a token, a secret or a sign-in session, so no cache may keep it. (This can only be one of no-store)
no-cache, the same instruction for HTTP/1.0 caches. (This can only be one of no-cache)

Signs the caller out and revokes the session behind the presented credential. The associated refresh token stops working as soon as this returns, so any subsequent authenticated call must start a fresh sign-in. Other active sessions for the same user are unaffected; remove those individually with the session-revocation call, or all at once with the revoke-other-sessions call.
Added as a part of security scheme: bearer

Completes passwordless email sign-in by redeeming the single-use token delivered by the magic-link start call. On success it returns an access and refresh token pair; the token is invalidated once consumed and cannot be replayed. Tokens are short-lived, so an expired or already-used link must be re-requested from the start call. A link to an account whose organization has since switched magic links off is refused with 403 auth.method_disabled and stays unused. A link that proves the account's address for the first time marks it verified, ends every earlier session and removes everything set up on the account before it, its password included (recorded as email.verified and auth.credentials_removed), so whoever registered the address first keeps no way in. The link proves the first factor only: when the account holds a second factor, or must have one, the answer is an MFA challenge instead of tokens, completed at POST /v1/auth/mfa (the session then records the method magic_link_mfa). The link is spent either way, so an abandoned or failed challenge leaves no tokens and no link to use again; an expired or used link is refused before any challenge is raised. A link to an address that must now sign in with single sign-on is refused with 403 auth.sso_required and stays unused (see the SSORequired response).

response.name: A token pair, or an MFA challenge to complete at POST /v1/auth/mfa

description.content: no-store: the response carries a token, a secret or a sign-in session, so no cache may keep it. (This can only be one of no-store)
no-cache, the same instruction for HTTP/1.0 caches. (This can only be one of no-cache)

Begins passwordless email sign-in by emailing a single-use link to the account holding the address. It answers the same whether or not the address has an account, takes the same minimum time, and sends nothing when it has none. The link is stored and emailed after the answer, so whether the email could be delivered does not change the answer either. An empty email is refused with 422 auth.email_required. Asked for from an organization's sign-in page (organization_id), it is refused with 403 auth.method_disabled when that organization has magic links off. Whichever organization asks, the account's own organization decides: nothing is sent when it has magic links off, a link lives for its magic_link_ttl_minutes, and a link stops working once it switches them off. A link works once; it goes to the address as the account stores it, and ends the earlier links to that address. With app hosted_login the link opens the hosted login's magic page and, once exchanged at the magic-link session call, continues the sign-in journey at return_to (kept only if it is this service's authorize endpoint); otherwise it opens the console's, exchanged at the consume call. Requests are bounded to three per address (then one every five minutes) and ten per caller (then one a minute), counted whether or not the address has an account: 429 past either. A link sent is recorded as auth.magic_link_requested in the audit trail of the account's own organization, and of the one that asked only if the account belongs to it, which alone brands the email; for anyone else it is the console's link. On a domain whose organization requires single sign-on, the request is refused with 403 auth.sso_required once counted against the bounds, before any account is looked up, and no link is sent (see the SSORequired response).

response.name: Accepted (always, to avoid account enumeration); returns a neutral confirmation message

description.content: Exchanges a magic link issued for the hosted login (app hosted_login) for the hosted-login session cookie, and returns where the sign-in journey continues (return_to, empty for none). The link works once: used, expired or unknown links, and console links, are refused (recovery.link_used, recovery.link_expired, recovery.magic_link_invalid), and so are links to an account whose organization has since switched magic links off. A link that proves the account's address for the first time marks it verified, ends every earlier session and removes everything set up on the account before it, its password included (recorded as email.verified and auth.credentials_removed), so whoever registered the address first keeps no way in. When the account holds a second factor, or must have one, no cookie is set: the answer is an MFA challenge (with return_to) completed at POST /v1/auth/session/mfa — on the same terms as the hosted password sign-in, including a trusted device (qe_td) skipping it where the organization allows. The link is spent either way. A link for an organization whose address rules refuse the browser's address answers 403 auth.address_not_allowed and opens no session. It is protected against cross-site requests as POST /v1/auth/session is (an allowed Origin, and the qe_csrf token echoed in X-CSRF-Token), and a body not sent as JSON is refused (415 unsupported_media_type). A link to an address that must now sign in with single sign-on is refused with 403 auth.sso_required and stays unused (see the SSORequired response).

response.name: Signed in to the hosted login (the cookie is set), or an MFA challenge to complete first

no-cache, the same instruction for HTTP/1.0 caches. (This can only be one of no-cache)

item.name: Magic link — send a new one

request.name: Magic link — send a new one

description.content: Sends a new sign-in link in place of the one a token names — used, expired or not — to the same address, opening in the same place and continuing the same journey, so the user need not type the address again. Answers the same whatever the token names, and is bounded like the start call (429). As there, the link is stored and emailed after the answer, so whether the email could be delivered does not change it. On a domain whose organization requires single sign-on, the resend is refused with 403 auth.sso_required and no link is sent (see the SSORequired response).

Returns the principal resolved from the presented credential, including the user, organization, and session identifiers, the actor type, and granted scopes. Use it to confirm who the current credential authenticates as and which organization it is scoped to. An organization-less principal reports a null organization until one is selected with the switch-organization call. Also accepts the hosted-login session cookie (qe_ls) in place of a bearer token, so a browser app signed in through the hosted login can tell who is signed in.
Added as a part of security scheme: bearer

Exchanges a valid refresh token for a new access and refresh token pair. The presented refresh token is rotated and invalidated, so each token may be redeemed only once; persist the returned refresh token for the next rotation. A revoked token is rejected and forces a fresh sign-in. A token presented again within the reuse grace of its rotation (REFRESH_TOKEN_REUSE_GRACE, 30 seconds by default, at most one minute), while the token that replaced it is still unused, gets the very pair its rotation returned, so two instances of a client renewing at once, or a client that lost the answer, keep the session; each such retry is audited as auth.refresh_token_retried. Any other reuse of a rotated token is treated as theft: the session ends (401 auth.session_revoked), audited as auth.token_reuse_detected. A session ends by itself at its maximum age however active it is, and once it goes longer than its idle timeout without a renewal; each renewal restarts the idle timeout, and the response says when the session ends either way (session_expires_at, idle_expires_at). A renewal after either is refused with 401 auth.session_timed_out and the session ends, recorded as an expiry and announced to session.revoked subscribers with the reason expired. A renewal from an address the organization's address rules refuse answers 403 auth.address_not_allowed; the session stays, and renews again from an allowed address. A session in a organization that has since been suspended or deleted is refused (403 auth.organization_inactive).
no-store: the response carries a token, a secret or a sign-in session, so no cache may keep it. (This can only be one of no-store)
no-cache, the same instruction for HTTP/1.0 caches. (This can only be one of no-cache)

Completes the password-reset flow started by the forgot-password call by consuming the emailed token and setting the new password. The token is single-use and time-limited, so an expired or already-redeemed token is rejected. The new password is checked against the rules of the organization the account belongs to (the platform baseline of 8 characters for an account with no organization), the offline strength baseline and, when enabled, the breached-password check; a refusal is a 422 naming the rule that failed and leaves the password and the token unchanged. On success the password is updated and the user can sign in with the new credentials. Every hosted sign-in (browser) session of the person ends too, so one opened with the old password can no longer start an application's sign-in or enrol a passkey; the audit record counts them (revoked_login_sessions). The completed reset is recorded in the account's organization's audit trail as auth.password_reset_confirmed. A reset that proves the account's address for the first time marks it verified and removes everything set up on the account before it but the new password (passkeys, second factors, linked accounts, pending verifications and sign-in codes, and personal API keys), so whoever registered the address first keeps no way in; recorded as email.verified and auth.credentials_removed. A link for an address that must now sign in with single sign-on is refused with 403 auth.sso_required; the password and the link stay as they were (see the SSORequired response). The account holder is emailed that it happened, with what to do if it wasn't them.

response.name: Password reset; returns a confirmation message

description.content: Signs the browser out of the hosted login: ends the hosted-login SSO session behind the qe_ls cookie and what it started — the refresh grants applications received through it are revoked and its unredeemed authorization codes can no longer be redeemed — then clears the cookie. The sign-out is recorded in the audit log (auth.signed_out). Other browsers, bearer-token API sessions and grants started elsewhere are unaffected; sign API sessions out with the logout call, or everything with sign out everywhere. Without a session cookie nothing is ended and the response is the same. If the sign-out cannot be completed an error is returned and the cookie kept, so it can be retried. Access tokens already issued stay valid until they expire.

response.name: Signed out (or there was no session to end), cookie cleared

description.content: no-store: the response carries a token, a secret or a sign-in session, so no cache may keep it. (This can only be one of no-store)
no-cache, the same instruction for HTTP/1.0 caches. (This can only be one of no-cache)

Establishes a hosted-login SSO session and sets the HttpOnly qe_ls cookie so the browser can continue into the OAuth authorize and consent flow. When the account has a second factor enrolled, no cookie is set yet and a short-lived mfa_token is returned; complete it at the session-MFA call before the cookie is issued. Because this is a cookie session, later state-changing calls made with it are subject to CSRF protection. End the session with the corresponding destroy-session call.

Sign-in lockout: failed password sign-ins are counted per account and source network (the client IP behind the trusted proxies; an IPv4 address or an IPv6 /64). Reaching the threshold within the window locks the account for that network for the lock duration, so a stranger on another network cannot lock the owner out. The threshold, window and duration are those of the organization of the OAuth client named by `client_id` (its authentication policy), or the platform defaults when no client is named. Failures from any mix of networks also lock the account everywhere at a looser cap (4 times the platform threshold), and a source network that fails against too many distinct accounts (30 within 15 minutes) is refused password sign-in for 15 minutes. An address with no account is counted and answered exactly like a wrong password, and so is a wrong password for a suspended or otherwise inactive account (401 auth.invalid_credentials); only the right password is refused with 403 auth.account_inactive. When the counters cannot be read or written the sign-in is refused with 503 auth.sign_in_unavailable (fail closed). When the organization of the named client_id has switched password sign-in off, the request is refused with 403 auth.method_disabled before any password is checked (the same answer for any account or none); without a client_id, the account's own organization decides once the password is verified. While the address rules of that client's organization are on, an address they refuse is answered 403 auth.address_not_allowed before any password is checked, and no cookie is set; the account's own organization's address rules then apply as well, whichever application asked, since the session reaches the account's self-service routes. A body not sent as JSON is refused (415 unsupported_media_type). Failed attempts are recorded as for POST /v1/auth/login. On a domain whose organization requires single sign-on, the sign-in is refused with 403 auth.sso_required before any account is looked up or password checked, and nothing is counted against the lockout (see the SSORequired response).

complete at POST /v1/auth/session/mfa — when the user holds a second
factor, or must have one (see MFAChallenge). No cookie is set until

Exchanges the mfa_token from POST /v1/auth/session, plus exactly one proof from the factors the challenge listed (a code, a passkey assertion, or an approved push — as for POST /v1/auth/mfa), for the SSO cookie (qe_ls). An enrolment challenge is completed by a code from the authenticator app set up for it, or skipped while its grace period runs, as for POST /v1/auth/mfa; a skipped setup never remembers the device. A body not sent as JSON is refused (415 unsupported_media_type). A wrong proof is recorded in the organization's audit trail as auth.sign_in_failed (method mfa, reason code_invalid, with the proof kind and the attempts left). Fifty wrong proofs in a row, however far apart, lock the person's second-factor sign-in: that answer and every later one is 403 mfa.locked, even with the right proof, the lock is audited as auth.mfa_locked and the person is emailed. A right proof ends a shorter run; a password reset, a password change or set, or an administrator's reset of their factors lifts the lock.

response.name: Second factor verified (or set up, or put off); SSO cookie set. recovery_codes are the account's new recovery codes when an authenticator app was just set up.

description.content: no-store: the response carries a token, a secret or a sign-in session, so no cache may keep it. (This can only be one of no-store)
no-cache, the same instruction for HTTP/1.0 caches. (This can only be one of no-cache)

Creates a new end-user in the client's organization and sets the SSO cookie
(qe_ls) so they continue into the OAuth authorize flow. Where the organization
requires MFA, no cookie is set: the response is an enrolment challenge
(with user_id) to complete at POST /v1/auth/session/mfa once an
authenticator app is set up. Gated by the
organization's self_registration_enabled policy (403 when disabled). The
password must meet that organization's password rules (422 naming the rule
that failed). An address that already has an account is refused with
the neutral 422 unprocessable of POST /v1/auth/signup, which does not
name the reason, and every attempt takes at least the same minimum time.
So is an address on a domain another organization has verified: only
that organization creates accounts there.

An address the organization's address rules refuse answers 403
auth.address_not_allowed, and no account is created.
A body not sent as JSON is refused (415 unsupported_media_type).
Where the organization has password sign-in switched off, it is refused with 403 auth.method_disabled (the answer password sign-in gives) and nothing is created.

On a domain whose organization requires single sign-on, the registration
is refused with 403 auth.sso_required before anything else is checked,
and nothing is created: the identity provider creates the account (see
the SSORequired response).

response.name: User created; SSO cookie set, or an enrolment challenge returned

description.content: no-store: the response carries a token, a secret or a sign-in session, so no cache may keep it. (This can only be one of no-store)
no-cache, the same instruction for HTTP/1.0 caches. (This can only be one of no-cache)

How many ways the caller's account can sign in: its password, each passkey, and each linked identity that can still sign in (a SAML or directory link, a social provider its organization has switched on, or a social account connected to the console account). Resetting a password by email is recovery and is not counted. Removing the last way — a passkey, a connected account, or an administrator unlinking an identity — is refused with 409 auth.last_sign_in_method and recorded (auth.sign_in_method_removal_refused); use total to disable or explain that action first.
Added as a part of security scheme: bearer
Reports whether the caller has a password set, so the account UI can offer "set a password" (social/passkey accounts) vs "change password".
Added as a part of security scheme: bearer

Rotates (or sets) the signed-in user's password. current_password is required only when one is already set; a social/passkey account may set one by omitting it. It needs a step-up while the caller holds a second factor (403 step_up_required), and otherwise a recent sign-in (403 recent_sign_in_required). Other sessions are revoked. The new password must meet the rules of the organization the account belongs to (not the session's organization; the platform baseline of 8 characters for an account with no organization), the offline strength baseline and, when enabled, the breached-password check; a refusal is a 422 naming the rule that failed. Self-service. Every hosted sign-in (browser) session of the person ends too, so one opened with the old password can no longer start an application's sign-in or enrol a passkey; the audit record counts them (revoked_login_sessions). The session the change is made from is kept. The account holder is emailed that it happened, with what to do if it wasn't them.
Added as a part of security scheme: bearer

Lists the caller's own remembered devices, in every organization, newest first: each device skips the second factor at sign-in until it expires or is forgotten. A device is remembered for its organization's remember_device_days after the sign-in that remembered it, and is forgotten when its owner changes their password, signs out everywhere, or has their factors reset.

response.name: OK

description.content: Added as a part of security scheme: bearer

description.content: Ends every one of the caller's sessions except the one they are using, in a single all-or-nothing step, and returns how many were ended. The session that is kept is the one behind the presented access token; the request takes no body and no session identifiers. The refresh and access tokens of the ended sessions stop working on this API as soon as this returns; a service that verifies access tokens offline, without introspection, accepts them until they expire (minutes). Succeeds with `revoked: 0` when there is no other session. If any session cannot be ended the call fails and none are ended. Returns 401 `auth.session_revoked` when the caller's own session has already ended. Sessions in hosted login and tokens held by applications are not affected; the sign-out-everywhere call ends those too.
Added as a part of security scheme: bearer

Signs the caller out everywhere in a single all-or-nothing step and reports how many sign-ins ended. It ends every one of the caller's sessions, including the one behind the presented access token; every hosted-login (browser) session, so the next authorization asks the person to sign in again; and every refresh grant held by applications the person signed in to. The response also clears the hosted-login cookie for a browser that calls directly. The request takes no body. Refresh tokens, application grants and the access tokens of the caller's own sessions stop working on this API as soon as this returns; access tokens held by applications, and any a service verifies offline, last until they expire (minutes). The presented access token must belong to one of the caller's own sessions (an application's access token is refused with 401). Repeating the call succeeds with every count at 0 and changes nothing. If anything cannot be ended the call fails and nothing is ended. To keep the current session, use the revoke-other-sessions call instead.

The password must meet the platform baseline (8 characters), the offline strength baseline and, when enabled, the breached-password check (422 naming the rule that failed). The new user is organization-less: no organization is created here, so the returned token carries no organization scope. Create an organization through the Identity Management API before any organization-scoped call, after which the creator becomes the organization owner. An address that already has an account is refused with a neutral 422 unprocessable that does not name the reason (it suggests signing in or resetting the password), every attempt takes at least the same minimum time, and the endpoint is rate limited. An address on a domain an organization has verified gets the same answer and no account: that organization creates its people's accounts. On a domain whose organization requires single sign-on, the sign-up is refused with 403 auth.sso_required before anything else is checked, and nothing is created: the identity provider creates the account (see the SSORequired response).

The session the presented access token belongs to ends: its refresh and access tokens are refused from now on, and the organization's session.revoked subscribers are notified with reason organization_switch. Use the returned pair from now on. The caller's session list shows the one sign-in, not one entry per switch. Begins a passkey sign-in ceremony and returns its session_id and the WebAuthn request options. Every ceremony is discoverable: the options carry no allowCredentials, and the answer is the same whether or not the email (optional; an empty body is allowed) has an account or a passkey. The browser that begins it is given an HttpOnly binding cookie (qe_passkey, __Host- prefixed outside dev) naming the ceremony; only that browser can finish it at POST /v1/passkeys/login/session. A body not sent as JSON is refused (415 unsupported_media_type). On a domain whose organization requires single sign-on, a ceremony begun with that email is refused with 403 auth.sso_required before the address is looked up (see the SSORequired response).

item.name: Ask for a code to link a phone

request.name: Ask for a code to link a phone

description.content: Issues a pairing code that links a phone running the mobile app to the caller's own account, so nobody copies an access token. The code is returned only in this response, shown grouped for reading (ABCDE-FGHJK); it links one phone, once, within five minutes, and asking for a new one stops the caller's earlier unused codes working. Needs a recent step-up when the caller already holds a second factor (403 step_up_required), and otherwise a recent sign-in (403 recent_sign_in_required). At most ten an hour (429 with retry_after). Audited as mfa.push_pairing_created. The phone exchanges the code with the claim call; the status call tells the screen showing it when it has been used.

description.content: Called by the mobile app, which holds no signed-in session, to link the phone it runs on to the account that asked for the pairing code. The code is read as typed or scanned: case, spaces and hyphens do not matter, and O, I and L read as 0, 1 and 1. Like registering a device, it returns the account's user_id, the device and its device_token, which is shown only here. description.content: Records the user's approval or denial of a push-MFA challenge, called by the enrolled device rather than the browser. It is authenticated by the device_token issued at registration together with the matching user_id, not a session credential, which is why no bearer token is required. An approval must carry the number shown where the request was asked for (the sign-in screen, or the step-up prompt); with another number the request is denied and the call answers 403 mfa.push_number_mismatch.

Pass explain=true to add the role grant paths, a reason on denial and the step-by-step trace. This is a read-only decision and changes no state.

Runs the deny-wins ABAC evaluation algorithm against all enabled policies
that match the supplied resource type and action. Returns the decision and,
when ?explain=true, a trace of every policy evaluated.
A deny policy whose condition compares an attribute the request doesn't
supply applies (fail closed); an allow policy doesn't match. Supply the
resource's attributes (such as created_by) for policies that compare them.
The platform's own decisions (the route guard, the permission and
relationship checks, AuthZEN) supply what it knows of the user, which a
caller can't override: subject.id, subject.type, subject.organization_id,
subject.groups and subject.roles (names in the organization; roles held
directly or through a group), resource.type and resource.id. The route
guard, deciding on the person's own call, also supplies context.ip (the
client address) and context.mfa: true when the session's sign-in met a
second factor as the organization's MFA requirement counts one (a
challenge, a passkey or a remembered device) or the session holds a step-up
still inside its window, false otherwise, and left out, so unknown, for an
application's token, whose session the platform doesn't hold.
With a draft, the unsaved policy is evaluated among the stored ones, new or
in place of the stored policy it replaces, and nothing is saved; an invalid
draft is refused with 422 as a save would be.

item.name: ReBAC
item.description: Relationship-based access control — relationship tuples and graph-based permission checks.

description.content:
List tuples anchored on one side of the relationship. Supply exactly one of:

OpenID AuthZEN core PDP evaluation request, answered by the same composed decision as the permission and relation checks (an ABAC deny refuses; then roles, relationships and ABAC allow policies are a union). When resource.type is "permission", action.name is the permission key; otherwise resource becomes "type:id" and action.name the relation. The response context always carries decided_by. ABAC policies see the request's properties, subject.properties as subject.*, resource.properties as resource.*, action.properties as action.*, and context (but for explain) as context.*. What the platform knows of the subject (id, type, organization_id, and for a person, groups and roles) wins over a property of the same name, as resource.type and resource.id and action.name win over theirs. A relationship check expands at most 1,000 distinct object#relation pairs, and a request's checks together read at most 5,000 relationship sets; past either it is refused with 422 rebac.check_too_complex.

OpenID AuthZEN access evaluations: several evaluations in one call, each answered as the single evaluation endpoint answers one. The top-level subject, resource, action and context are defaults; an evaluation that names one of them replaces it whole. Decisions come back in the request's order. options.evaluations_semantic is execute_all (the default), deny_on_first_deny, which stops after the first deny, or permit_on_first_permit, which stops after the first permit; the response then holds the evaluations up to that one. An evaluation the caller got wrong, such as one without a subject id, is denied with context.error {status, code, message} and counts as a deny. At most 100 evaluations (more is 422 authzen.too_many_evaluations); an unknown semantic is 422 authzen.evaluations_semantic_invalid. Without evaluations, the request is a single evaluation and the response is a single decision. Each relationship check expands at most 1,000 distinct object#relation pairs, and the request's checks together read at most 5,000 relationship sets: an evaluation past either is denied with context.error rebac.check_too_complex (422). Requires role.read.
(Required) The organization's ID. On an authenticated route it must be the organization of the caller's credential: another is refused with 403, and a value that is not a UUID with 400.

Turns the organization's address rules on or off ({"enabled": bool}). While they are on, every sign-in to the organization (password, passkey, magic link, social, SAML, LDAP, invitation, organization switch, application authorization, device approval and the device's token collection) and every session renewal asks them first. An address is refused when a deny rule matches it, or when allow rules exist and none matches; deny wins. An address that can't be read is refused. A refusal answers 403 auth.address_not_allowed (access_denied to an application), names no rule, and is audited as auth.address_refused with the rule responsible, the address and the path. Off, nothing is checked. Switching them on is refused with 409 risk.rules_lock_out_caller when they would refuse the address the request comes from (as are adding or removing a rule while they are on, when the result would), so an admin can't lock themselves out; the console calls from its own server, so its address must stay allowed. Qeet ID — Identity Management API

Organizations, domains, users, groups, and invitations for Qeet ID.

## Start here — the organization lifecycle

1. A newly registered user has **no organization**. Create one with `POST /v1/organizations`; the caller becomes the organization **owner**.
2. (Optional) Prove control of a domain under **Domains** to unlock domain-based features.
3. Add and manage users, organize them into groups, and invite teammates.

The `register → organization-less user → create organization → owner` sequence is the most common early surprise: authentication happens in the Authentication & Access API; organization creation happens here.

## Authentication

Auth modes: `bearerAuth` (user/service JWT), `apiKeyAuth` (`Authorization: ApiKey <key>` — legacy scheme), `scimBearer` (per-organization SCIM token), `clientCredentials` (OAuth M2M), and `ssoCookie` (hosted-login SSO session). CSRF protection applies only to cookie sessions (`ssoCookie`): requests authorised by `bearerAuth` or `apiKeyAuth` bypass it, as do the token endpoint (POST /v1/oauth/token) and the directory sign-in (POST /ldap/{id}/authenticate), which carry their credentials in the request. Basic credentials do not bypass it. A request that fails the check is refused with 403 `csrf_failed`.

The responses of organization creation and invitation acceptance, including accepting with an existing account (sign-in tokens), are sent with `Cache-Control: no-store` and `Pragma: no-cache`.

Every response carries an `X-Request-Id` header naming the request; quote it when reporting a problem. An error body repeats it as `error.request_id`. A path with an encoded slash or backslash (`%2F`, `%5C`) is refused with 400 `bad_request`.

## Related APIs

- **Authentication & Access API** — login, passkeys, MFA, authorization
- **Federation API** — OIDC/OAuth provider, SAML, SCIM, LDAP, social
- **Developer API** — API keys, agents, webhooks, vaults
- **Operations API** — audit, analytics, billing

## Contract maintenance

This document covers routes mounted by internal/bootstrap/router.go. internal/bootstrap/openapi_coverage_test.go walks the production mount helpers and fails when a mounted operation is undocumented, a documented operation is stale, or API-auth security declarations disagree with runtime classification.

Soft-deletes the user, moving the account into the organization recycle bin rather than erasing it. Requires user.delete. A soft-deleted account can be brought back with the restore call or removed for good with the purge call. It continues to appear in the deleted-users list until purged. In the same transaction every way the user is signed in ends (sessions, hosted-login sessions, application grants, remembered devices and pending authorizations), the deletion is audited (user.deleted, naming the admin) and a user.deleted event is queued; restoring the account brings none of those sessions back. The same transaction revokes the admin-portal links and pending invitations the user issued here and, when they created any integration here that still works (a service principal, SCIM token, webhook, auth hook or OIDC application), records the critical user.integrations_left event listing them for review. A pending invitation holds a seat, as does each person holding a role, directly or through a group; when the plan's seats are all taken the invitation is refused with 402 billing.plan_limit (metadata resource seats, limit), and accepting it later takes no further seat. An invitation a person sent is accepted only while they still may give it: active, still in the organization and able to give its role, or acceptance is refused with 400 invite.invalid; removing them from the organization or deleting their account withdraws the invitations they sent. Qeet ID — Federation API (OIDC/SAML/SCIM/LDAP/Social)

OAuth 2.0 / OIDC provider, social login, SAML, LDAP, and SCIM for Qeet ID.

## Start here

Qeet ID federates in both directions — know which role applies:

- **Qeet ID → your app:** OIDC provider and SAML **Identity Provider**.
- **External IdP → Qeet ID:** SAML **Service Provider**, **OpenID Connect relying party** for an organization's own provider, **LDAP** client, and **OAuth client** for social logins.
- **External IdP → Qeet ID (provisioning):** **SCIM** server.

## One OAuth token endpoint

`POST /v1/oauth/token`, which discovery advertises as the `token_endpoint`, serves every grant, chosen by `grant_type`: authorization_code, refresh_token, device_code, token-exchange and CIBA for applications, and client_credentials for service principals and AI agents.

## Path prefixes

Discovery (`/.well-known/*`), `/oauth/revoke`, `/oauth/introspect`, `/scim/v2/*`, `/saml/*`, and `/ldap/*` are mounted at the **root**, not under `/v1`. Interactive OAuth endpoints (`/v1/oauth/*`) are under `/v1`.

## Authentication

Auth modes: `bearerAuth` (user/service JWT), `apiKeyAuth` (`Authorization: ApiKey <key>` — legacy scheme), `scimBearer` (per-organization SCIM token), `clientCredentials` (OAuth M2M), and `ssoCookie` (hosted-login SSO session). CSRF protection applies only to cookie sessions (`ssoCookie`): requests authorised by `bearerAuth` or `apiKeyAuth` bypass it, as do the token endpoint (POST /v1/oauth/token) and the directory sign-in (POST /ldap/{id}/authenticate), which carry their credentials in the request. Basic credentials do not bypass it. A request that fails the check is refused with 403 `csrf_failed`.

The responses of the token endpoint, device and back-channel authorization, the consent decision (an authorization code), directory sign-in, social, SAML and OpenID Connect connection code exchange, the SAML IdP's sign-on page (a signed assertion), and of the operations returning a new client secret, service-principal credential, SCIM token or admin-portal link, are sent with `Cache-Control: no-store` and `Pragma: no-cache`.

Every response carries an `X-Request-Id` header naming the request; quote it when reporting a problem. An error body repeats it as `error.request_id`. A path with an encoded slash or backslash (`%2F`, `%5C`) is refused with 400 `bad_request`.

## Related APIs

- **Authentication & Access API** — login, passkeys, MFA, authorization
- **Identity Management API** — organizations, users, groups, invitations
- **Developer API** — API keys, agents, webhooks, vaults
- **Operations API** — audit, analytics, billing

## Contract maintenance

This document covers routes mounted by internal/bootstrap/router.go. internal/bootstrap/openapi_coverage_test.go walks the production mount helpers and fails when a mounted operation is undocumented, a documented operation is stale, or API-auth security declarations disagree with runtime classification.

item.name: OIDC
item.description: OpenID Connect / OAuth 2.0 provider: discovery, authorize, token, userinfo, clients, grants, revocation, introspection, RP-initiated logout, and machine-to-machine service principals.

description.content: Publishes the issuer's public signing keys as a JWK Set so relying parties and resource servers can verify Qeet-issued ID tokens and JWT access tokens, with Qeet acting as the OpenID provider. Served unauthenticated at the root, not under /v1, and advertised as jwks_uri in the discovery document. Keys rotate, so callers should cache by key id and refetch when they encounter an unknown one. Any origin may read it (CORS Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *, without credentials).

Returns the OpenID Connect discovery metadata for Qeet as the OpenID provider: issuer, authorization, token, userinfo, JWKS, revocation, introspection and end-session endpoints, plus the supported grant types, scopes (openid, profile, email, phone and offline_access) and algorithms. The advertised token_endpoint is /v1/oauth/token, which serves every grant, client_credentials for the service principals and agents included. Served unauthenticated at the root, not under /v1. Its issuer is the one the ID tokens and authorization responses carry (JWT_ISSUER). Any origin may read it (CORS Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *, without credentials).

Returns the OAuth 2.0 authorization server metadata (RFC 8414) for clients that speak only OAuth, and for model-context-protocol clients following the protected-resource document to the authorization server it names. It is the same document as the OpenID configuration, so the endpoints and capabilities in the two always agree. Served unauthenticated at the root, not under /v1.

Protected-resource metadata (RFC 9728) for MCP authorization-server compliance. Advertises the resource identifier, its authorization server(s), the scopes it accepts (scopes_supported), and the supported bearer methods and token-signing algorithms. The authorization server is named by its issuer identifier (JWT_ISSUER, the iss of its tokens), whatever host the request reached, and resolves to its RFC 8414 metadata at /.well-known/oauth-authorization-server.

Reports whether a supplied access or refresh token is currently active and returns its associated claims when it is (RFC 7662), with Qeet acting as the OAuth authorization server. Callers authenticate with OAuth client credentials supplied as form parameters or via HTTP Basic. Mounted at the root, not under /v1; it pairs with the revocation endpoint for token lifecycle management. A public client can't call it: its client_id is in every sign-in link and proves nothing, so the call answers 401 oidc.client_auth_failed. Wrong secrets are audited. An application only learns about tokens it owns: an access token issued to it (its client_id claim), or one issued for a registered resource it serves (server_client_id), and a refresh token issued to it. Any other token, including another application's in the same organization or one from another organization, answers only {"active": false}, so the endpoint never confirms a token exists; asking about another application's token is audited as oidc.introspection_refused. An active access token reports its real aud (a string for one audience, a list for several), its client_id, and resource when it was issued for one. Introspection is the authoritative answer on revocation: a signature-valid access token whose account is suspended or deleted, whose membership of the organization has ended, whose sign-in has ended, or whose agent is no longer active, answers {"active": false}. The sign-in is the session the token names in sid: a person's own session, or for an application's token the hosted-login session it was issued in, ended by signing out of it (one that only expired still renews through its grant). Device and backchannel tokens name no session. A verifier that checks tokens offline (signature and expiry) accepts such a token until it expires (ACCESS_TOKEN_TTL, 10 minutes by default); call introspection where revocation must take effect at once. A browser may call it from an origin one of the applications allows (web_origins), without credentials.

Begins the OAuth 2.0 / OpenID Connect authorization-code flow with Qeet as the provider. The end user is identified by the hosted-login SSO session cookie: with no session the browser is redirected to the hosted login, with the qe_sc cookie naming the application (an hour, HttpOnly, cleared once a code is issued) so the sign-in that follows records it in its auth.login_succeeded event (client_id, client_name), with missing consent to the hosted consent screen, and otherwise back to the client's redirect_uri carrying an authorization code and state. Exchange that code for tokens at the token endpoint (authorization_code grant). The redirect_uri must be one the client registered, character for character, except that a public (native) client's http redirect to a loopback IP literal (such as http://127.0.0.1/cb or http://[::1]/cb) may name any port (RFC 8252 §7.3), as a native application listens on whatever port it is given; a confidential client's matches exactly, and localhost is a name, not a literal, and matches exactly. Otherwise the error is shown here and nothing is sent to that address. The code goes to the redirect_uri as requested, port included, and redeems only with that same redirect_uri. When consent is needed, the request is stored server-side and the hosted consent screen is given only its request_id. While the client organization's address rules are on, a browser address they refuse gets access_denied at the redirect_uri and no code, and the refusal is audited (auth.address_refused). Every application, confidential ones included, must send a PKCE code_challenge with code_challenge_method S256; a request without one gets invalid_request at the redirect_uri (oidc.code_challenge_required) before any consent is asked. A confidential application whose pkce_exempt_until is still ahead is excused until then. The challenge binds the code to the request, so a nonce is optional (OpenID Connect Core 3.1.2.1); one that is sent comes back in the ID token. response_type is required and only code is served (else invalid_request / unsupported_response_type at the redirect_uri); request and request_uri are refused (request_not_supported, request_uri_not_supported), as is a response_mode other than query. prompt=none never shows a page: no sign-in answers login_required, no consent consent_required. prompt=login, and a sign-in older than max_age seconds, send the browser to sign in again and then complete the request (the request it comes back with carries a login_after marker the server signs, so one added by hand doesn't stand for the sign-in); prompt=consent asks for consent again. The ID token carries auth_time (when the person signed in) and sid (the hosted-login session). When the client's organization requires a second factor the hosted sign-in didn't meet, the browser is sent to sign in again for this request (where the hosted login asks for it), once; prompt=none answers interaction_required, and a fresh sign-in that still hasn't met one gets access_denied at the redirect_uri.

Performs OpenID Connect RP-initiated logout: ends the hosted-login SSO session behind the qe_ls cookie and what it started — the refresh grants applications received through it are revoked and its unredeemed authorization codes can no longer be redeemed — and clears the cookie. Only the cookie identifies the session to end; without it nothing is ended. The sign-out is recorded in the audit log (auth.signed_out), naming client_id when it is a registered application. When the client supplies a registered post_logout_redirect_uri the browser is redirected there with any provided state; otherwise the hosted logged-out page is shown. Other browsers and API sessions are unaffected. Advertised as end_session_endpoint in discovery; a POST variant exists at the same path for relying parties that submit the request as a form. A sign-out must carry an id_token_hint (one of our ID tokens, expired or not, issued to a registered application, client_id when given, for this session's person and naming this session when it names one; another session's, and any other token this server signs, such as an access token or a sign-in ticket, is refused with 400 invalid_request) or a logout_confirmation ticket: without either, the browser is sent to the hosted login's /sign-out page to confirm, with a ticket that brings it back, so a plain link or image can't sign anyone out. Every application that holds a code or grant from the ended session is told: a signed logout token (OpenID Connect Back-Channel Logout 1.0, with sid) is POSTed to its backchannel_logout_uri and retried with backoff, a final failure audited as oidc.backchannel_logout_failed; its frontchannel_logout_uri (with iss and sid) is given to the hosted signed-out page, which then continues to the post_logout_redirect_uri through /v1/oauth/logout/continue. Audited as oidc.sign_out_notified.

The OAuth token endpoint (RFC 6749 §3.2) advertised in discovery, the one for every grant, chosen by grant_type: authorization_code, refresh_token, device_code (RFC 8628), token-exchange (RFC 8693) and CIBA with Qeet as the authorization server, and client_credentials for the machine identities. Clients authenticate with their credentials in the form body or via HTTP Basic. Errors take the RFC 6749 §5.2 shape (error, error_description): a missing grant_type is invalid_request, an unknown grant unsupported_grant_type, and a grant the client may not use unauthorized_client. A missing or wrong secret, or an unknown client_id, is refused with 401 invalid_client, described the same whatever kind of client the id names, with WWW-Authenticate: Basic when the client used HTTP Basic. The client_credentials grant serves service principals and AI agents: client_id is the principal's or agent's id and client_secret its secret. It answers a token for the identity itself, carrying every scope it holds (scope is ignored), marked actor_type service or agent (an agent's also agent_id), lasting the access-token lifetime for a principal and the agent's own token_ttl_seconds for an agent, with expires_at beside expires_in. A disabled principal or an agent that isn't active is refused with unauthorized_client once its secret checks out, a principal or agent of a suspended or deleted organization as an unknown client, and an application (an OIDC client) with unauthorized_client once its own credentials check out. Every grant refuses an account that is suspended or deleted with invalid_grant, and a refused refresh ends the application's refresh tokens for that user. Device polling from an address the organization's address rules refuse answers access_denied address_not_allowed and spends the device code; code redemption, refresh and CIBA polling come from the application's server, so the address rules are asked at authorization or approval instead. An authorization code redeems once, with the code_verifier of its challenge; a code issued under a PKCE exemption redeems only while the exemption lasts. A code presented a second time is refused with invalid_grant and the grant its first redemption issued is revoked, every renewal of it included (audited as oidc.authorization_code_reused). Token exchange (RFC 8693) is bounded: the caller must be entitled to the subject token (issued to it, issued for a registered resource it serves, or the person consented to it; else invalid_request), the person must still be active and the organization live (else invalid_grant), the result expires no later than the subject token, carries a new session id, and records its exchange_depth; a token two exchanges deep can't be exchanged again (invalid_request). Every exchange is audited as oidc.token_exchanged; the result holds at most the subject token's scopes that the caller is registered for and, when it holds the token by the person's consent, that they consented to; a scope beyond those is invalid_scope. A refresh token comes only to an application registered for refresh_token, on the authorization_code, device_code and CIBA grants: with every grant, unless the application lists offline_access among its scopes, in which case only with a grant of offline_access (OpenID Connect Core §11). The ID token a refresh issues again reports the original sign-in, as OpenID Connect Core 12.2 asks: the same auth_time and sid as the first one, and no nonce. A refresh may name only the resource (RFC 8707) its grant is bound to: another is refused with 400 invalid_target, and naming none carries the bound resource forward. The client_credentials, device_code and CIBA grants take no resource: one sent is refused with invalid_target. Device and CIBA polling authenticate the client as the other grants do; a public client is identified by its client_id, and the device_code or auth_req_id is the proof (CIBA serves confidential clients only). The per-address rate limit answers 429 too_many_requests in the error envelope. A refresh is refused with unauthorized_client when the client is no longer registered for refresh_token, and with invalid_grant once the person is no longer an active member of the client's organization (its own account, or one holding a role there) or the organization is suspended. A refresh carries forward only the granted scopes the client still registers (scope in the response says which) and is refused with invalid_scope when none is left. The same membership is required when a code, device approval or backchannel request is redeemed (a code, device code or backchannel request refused so is spent). A code, device code or backchannel approval is refused with unauthorized_client once its client is no longer registered for that grant, and a backchannel approval also once its client is no longer a confidential one. A device code or backchannel request is spent only together with storing its refresh token, so a failure leaves it for the next poll. A browser may call it from an origin one of the applications allows (web_origins), without credentials.

Send an Idempotency-Key header to retry it safely: a retry with the same key and body within 24 hours gets the first answer, marked Idempotent-Replayed: true; the same key with another body answers 422 idempotency.key_reused, one still being processed 409 idempotency.in_progress, and one whose first request stopped before answering 409 idempotency.outcome_unknown: check whether it took effect, then retry with a new key. description.content: Trades the one-time code a social sign-in callback handed back (the console's own, or an organization's) for the sign-in's result. Social sign-in takes the same second-factor decision as a password sign-in: the response is a token pair, or, when the account holds a second factor, the organization requires one, or the sign-in is risky, the challenge instead (mfa_required, mfa_token, methods, factors, and enrollment_required for an account that must set one up), completed at POST /v1/auth/mfa. description.content: Attaches the provider identity a link callback returned, held under the one-time link_code the account page was sent back with, to the caller. Only the account that began the link (POST /v1/social/{provider}/link/start) completes it; for any other the code is spent and the answer is 403 social.link_account_mismatch, so a connect link sent to someone else never attaches their provider account to the sender's. An unknown, used or expired code answers 400 social.link_code_invalid (codes live two minutes); an identity already linked to another account answers 409 social.already_linked. An account whose organization requires single sign-on on its domain links no provider (403 auth.sso_required), as no social sign-in signs it in.

Adds a social provider, or replaces the settings of one the organization already has. Replacing keeps whether the provider is switched on, and an empty client_secret keeps the stored one. The secret is stored encrypted and never returned. A provider named github, facebook, x, discord or apple uses that provider's own OAuth 2.0 flow and needs no discovery URL (kind names it); any other name is an OpenID Connect provider found by discovery_url. For apple, client_id is the Services ID and client_secret the .p8 private key with apple_team_id and apple_key_id: the server signs Apple's short-lived client secret from them for each sign-in, and a key that can't sign one is refused with 422. X signs in with PKCE. An address from GitHub, X (confirmed_email) or Discord (verified) counts as verified; one from Facebook doesn't, so it can make a new account but never sign in to an existing one by its address. An OpenID Connect provider's endpoints are the organization's choice, so its word verifies an address only on a domain the organization has verified: elsewhere it too can make a new account, its address unverified, but never sign in to an existing one by its address. Audited as social_provider.created or social_provider.updated (the fields saved and whether the secret was replaced, never its value). Changing what the connection trusts (an OpenID Connect provider's discovery_url, including setting one up again under a name it had before) is acting on every account linked to it, as the changed connection could sign in as any of them: while an administrator is linked, it needs a caller who outranks each one (403 rbac.trust_change_outranks_caller otherwise).

Changes only the fields given on one of the caller's organization's social providers — switch it off or on, replace its secret, or change its client ID or discovery URL. Takes effect for the next sign-in; other providers are unaffected. A switched-off provider reads to a signing-in user exactly like one that was never set up. Audited as social_provider.updated (fields changed, whether the secret was replaced), social_provider.disabled and social_provider.enabled. 404 for a provider the organization does not have. Switching it off is refused with 409 social.provider_in_use (metadata.people: how many) while anyone in the organization can sign in only through it, as removing it is; give them another way in first. Changing what the connection trusts (an OpenID Connect provider's discovery_url) is acting on every account linked to it, as the changed connection could sign in as any of them: while an administrator is linked, it needs a caller who outranks each one (403 rbac.trust_change_outranks_caller otherwise).

Removes one of the caller's organization's social providers. The identities people linked through it are kept — they still show in those people's connected accounts and work again if the provider is added back — but nobody can sign in through it meanwhile. Refused with 409 social.provider_in_use (metadata.people: how many) while anyone in the organization can sign in only through it (no password, no passkey, no other linked identity); give them another way in first. Completes a social sign-in: exchanges the provider's code, then signs in the account linked to that provider identity, adopts the organization's existing account for a verified address, or creates an account. The callback completes only in the browser that began the sign-in, which holds the binding cookie from GET /v1/social/{provider}/start: the same return link opened in another browser, or without the cookie, is refused and nothing is issued — the browser is sent to the hosted login with error=other_browser and the return_to (the console flow gets social_error=other_browser). A link ceremony (POST /v1/social/{provider}/link/start) attaches nothing here: the browser is sent to the account page with a one-time link_code and the provider, which the account that began the link completes at POST /v1/social/link/complete. Creating one is self-registration: when the organization does not allow it, nothing is created, the attempt is audited (social.signup_refused, naming the provider and the address), and the browser is sent to the hosted login with error=registration_closed and the original return_to. Nor is an account created on a domain another organization has verified, or on one whose organization requires single sign-on (error=social). The console's own sign-up (intent=signup) creates no account on a domain an organization has verified either (error=social). An address the organization's address rules refuse is sent there with error=address_not_allowed and the return_to, and no hosted-login session is opened. An existing account whose address has never been verified, unless the organization's directory provisioned it (SCIM), is not adopted by the provider's word (error=account_unverified; the console flow gets social_error=account_unverified): it must verify the address, or reset its password from the emailed link, first. An OpenID Connect provider's word counts as verified only for an address on a domain the organization has verified (see POST /v1/social/providers). A suspended or deleted account gets error=account_inactive (the console flow gets social_error=account_inactive). When the sign-in must meet a second factor first (the account holds one, the organization requires one, or the sign-in is risky; a remembered device may skip it as for a password sign-in), no hosted-login session is opened either: the browser is sent to the hosted login with the return_to, and the challenge in the URL fragment (mfa_token, methods, factors — the JSON list a password sign-in's challenge carries, with an email or SMS factor's id and masked destination — and enrollment_required / enrollment_due_at for one to set up), to complete at POST /v1/auth/session/mfa. Other failures send it there with error=social. An organization's own provider signs in only an account whose home is that organization, whether linked before or adopted by email. Neither it nor the console's own sign-in signs in, adopts or links an account on a domain whose organization requires single sign-on, except its break-glass members (error=social; the console flow gets the same): only that organization's identity provider signs its people in. Nor does any provider adopt by email an account that owns or administers the organization (social.account_administers; the browser gets error=social): it keeps its own credentials and connects the provider from its account.

item.name: SAML
item.description: SAML 2.0 SSO — Qeet as Service Provider (consuming external IdPs) and as Identity Provider (serving downstream SPs).

description.content: The SAML Assertion Consumer Service for a specific connection, with Qeet acting as the Service Provider. It validates the external IdP's signed SAMLResponse and assertion (an EncryptedAssertion is decrypted with the connection's SP key first and must still be signed; signature by any of the certificates the connection trusts; conditions, allowing three minutes of clock difference with the IdP either way; and replay protection), provisions or resolves the user just-in-time, and redirects to the SPA callback with a one-time login code carried in the URL fragment. An answer to a sign-in request completes only in the browser that began it (holding the cookie the login call set): from another it spends the request and answers 403 saml.other_browser, so a sign-in begun by someone else can't be completed in a victim's browser. An IdP-initiated answer, which answers no request, is accepted only where the connection allows those. The SPA then trades that code for tokens at POST /saml/exchange. Mounted at the root, not under /v1, and unauthenticated. An existing account is signed in only while this organization is its home, and one adopted by email must have a verified address or have been provisioned by the organization's directory (SCIM), and is then marked verified: another organization's account or a guest whose home is elsewhere is refused with 403 saml.user_organization_mismatch, an unverified one with 403 saml.account_unverified. A subject is linked to the connection that asserted it, so another connection asserting it doesn't sign it in. An address not yet linked is adopted or given an account only on a domain the organization has verified (the most specific verified domain decides, 403 saml.email_domain_unverified otherwise), and an account that owns the organization or holds any permission there but the reads organization.read, user.read, role.read, group.read, connection.read, apikey.read, webhook.read, billing.read, policy.read, audit.read and analytics.read is not adopted by its address (403 saml.account_administers): it keeps its own credentials. A new account is created only while the domain that manages the address has jit_enabled on; otherwise an address with no account is refused with 403 saml.jit_not_allowed and nothing is created. Existing members are adopted either way. Every sign-in then brings the account in step with the assertion, each change audited: its display name; its address, when the asserted one is on a domain the organization has verified, is no other account's, and the account doesn't administer the organization (recovery links sent to the old address then stop working); and its groups, as GET /v1/organizations/{organizationID}/saml/{id}/group-mappings describes. The organization's plan must include enterprise SSO when the assertion arrives, so a connection set up on a plan that has since lapsed signs no one in (402 billing.upgrade_required). A failure of a sign-in the hosted login began (its return_to stored with the request, named by the answer once it is bound to this browser, or else by this browser's binding cookie) redirects instead to the hosted login's /sign-in with a generic error (sso, or account_inactive for a suspended or deleted account) and the same return_to; the detail is logged, never shown.
(Required)

Trades the one-time login code minted by the SAML Assertion Consumer Service for a Qeet access and refresh token pair, with Qeet acting as the Service Provider. The code is single-use and short-lived. It trades only while the connection that issued it is still active: 403 saml.connection_disabled or saml.connection_draft once it has been switched off or put back to draft, and 401 saml.login_code_invalid once it is deleted. Mounted at the root, not under /v1, and unauthenticated; it is the second step after POST /saml/acs/{id}.
no-store: the response carries a token, a secret or a sign-in session, so no cache may keep it. (This can only be one of no-store)
no-cache, the same instruction for HTTP/1.0 caches. (This can only be one of no-cache)

Trades the one-time login code a hosted-login SAML sign-in came back with (the hosted login's /sign-in URL fragment, saml_code) for the hosted-login session, as POST /v1/auth/session answers: the qe_ls cookie and the user's id. The code is single-use and short-lived (401 saml.login_code_invalid, saml.login_code_used or saml.login_code_expired), and trades only while the connection that issued it is still active (403 saml.connection_disabled or saml.connection_draft; 401 saml.login_code_invalid once it is deleted). The organization's network rules apply (403 auth.address_not_allowed), and an account that is not active is refused (403 auth.account_inactive). As the console's SAML sign-in, no second factor is asked: the identity provider decides how its people sign in. The session is recorded as a saml sign-in. Mounted at the root, not under /v1, and unauthenticated; CSRF-checked.

Mounted at the root, not under /v1, and unauthenticated. An unknown or inactive organization returns 404. Register each downstream SP with the SAML SP (IdP side) endpoints before it can obtain assertions at the organization's IdP SSO endpoint.

Returns the certificate the organization's SAML Identity Provider signs assertions with, as PEM, the same one its metadata publishes, for Service Providers that ask for the certificate on its own. Mounted at the root, not under /v1, and unauthenticated. An unknown or inactive organization returns 404.
(Required) The organization's ID. On an authenticated route it must be the organization of the caller's credential: another is refused with 403, and a value that is not a UUID with 400.
